claims.text: Group IV-containing refractory HEA hydride powders have high internal strain.
The hydride powders have high surface area and are susceptible to rapid oxidation upon heating.
The powder should be cold-pressed into a green body and thermally decomposed in a sealed, evacuated extrusion die before immediate hot extrusion without ambient exposure.
Hydride decomposition and hydrogen desorption should be initiated by heating to 400°C at 5°C/min under a pressure of 10^-4 Pa.
The material should then be rapidly heated to 0.85 T_melt, approximately 1400–1600°C depending on the alloy, and held for 30 minutes under 10^-7 Pa before extrusion pressure is applied.
Oxygen partial pressure must remain below 10^-10 Pa throughout processing.
The proposed thermal and vacuum history will suppress oxygen diffusion into the metal lattice.
The proposed process will kinetically inhibit nucleation and growth of brittle alpha-HCP material.
The proposed process will maintain a single-phase metastable BCC solid solution.
Rapid hydrogen removal at low temperature prevents formation of oxygen-stabilized surface oxides that would act as alpha-HCP nucleation sites.
An ultra-high-vacuum high-temperature hold facilitates solid-state sintering and dynamic recrystallization of the BCC phase.
Extremely low oxygen partial pressure thermodynamically disfavors stable oxide formation and kinetically limits the oxygen diffusion required for HCP transformation.
Extrusion pressure enables densification without prolonged high-temperature exposure that would permit oxygen ingress.
The process will produce a bulk material with greater than 98% of theoretical density.
The processed bulk will undergo no catastrophic cracking.
The processed bulk will have a ductile-to-brittle transition temperature below room temperature.
At 1000°C, the processed bulk will have 20–30% higher yield strength than conventionally processed alloys.
Retention of a fine-grained, oxygen-free BCC structure without brittle HCP precipitates causes the predicted increase in high-temperature yield strength.
Conventional hydride decomposition in Ar or air followed by sintering and extrusion typically causes oxygen uptake, alpha-HCP precipitation, elevated transition temperatures, and extrusion cracking.
